papers.core_contribution: Attention heads that promote factual output in LLMs operate via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, and their behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models showing more specialization.
papers.conclusion: The study confirms that attention heads mediate the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens via copy suppression, and their effects are domain-dependent, with implications for model interpretability and control.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads contribute to the competition between factual and counterfactual tokens, and modifying their strength affects the proportion of factual outputs.
The attention heads supporting factual tokens suppress copying in general, not just counterfactuals, as they also suppress factual tokens when facts are present in the prompt.
The effect of attention heads is sensitive to sentence structure and the presence of hints (factual token in the subject).
Attention heads exhibit domain specialization; their contribution varies by answer category (e.g., location, language, organization).
Larger models (Pythia-6.9B) show more specialized and category-sensitive patterns than smaller models (GPT-2).
papers.limitation: The experiments are limited to two models (GPT-2 and Pythia-6.9B) and do not cover more models or study attention modification of different heads on different domains in detail.
future_direction: Applying the methods to different models
Studying how each attention head interacts with different domains
Constructing new datasets on other domains (e.g., STEM) and applying similar techniques
papers.abstract: This paper presents a reproducibility study examining how Large Language Models (LLMs) manage competing factual and counterfactual information, focusing on the role of attention heads in this process. We attempt to reproduce and reconcile findings from three recent studies by Ortu et al., Yu, Merullo, and Pavlick and McDougall et al. that investigate the competition between model-learned facts and contradictory context information through Mechanistic Interpretability tools. Our study specifically examines the relationship between attention head strength and factual output ratios, evaluates competing hypotheses about attention heads' suppression mechanisms, and investigates the domain specificity of these attention patterns. Our findings suggest that attention heads promoting factual output do so via general copy suppression rather than selective counterfactual suppression, as strengthening them can also inhibit correct facts. Additionally, we show that attention head behavior is domain-dependent, with larger models exhibiting more specialized and category-sensitive patterns.

papers.title: On the Reasoning Capacity of AI Models and How to Quantify It
papers.research_question: This paper investigates the reasoning capacity of AI models, specifically how to quantify and distinguish between genuine reasoning and other cognitive processes like memorization and guessing in large language models.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a phenomenological framework that decomposes model behavior into reasoning, memorization, and guessing components, showing that accuracy alone often overstates reasoning abilities and that models rely on sophisticated combinations of memorization and pattern matching.
papers.conclusion: This work introduces a new phenomenological approach to evaluating reasoning in language models, demonstrating that controlled experimentation can reveal deeper insights into model behavior and providing tools for more reliable evaluation methodologies.
papers.key_findings:
True reasoning remains challenging for current models, with apparent success often relying on memorization and pattern matching rather than genuine logical deduction.
Positional bias in multiple-choice tasks can reveal fundamental aspects of model decision-making and strategy selection.
The probabilistic mixture model quantitatively decomposes model responses into reasoning, memorization, and guessing probabilities.
Information-theoretic consistency analysis shows relationships between model confidence and strategy selection, with models often overconfident in low-accuracy regimes.
The framework enables quantitative criteria for model deployment based on strategy distributions rather than aggregate accuracy.
future_direction: Expanding the approach to examine other forms of systematic bias beyond positional effects.
Deeper theoretical investigation into the mathematical structures governing model responses.
Creating more nuanced benchmarks and evaluation methods based on strategy interplay.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) have intensified the debate surrounding the fundamental nature of their reasoning capabilities. While achieving high performance on benchmarks such as GPQA and MMLU, these models exhibit limitations in more complex reasoning tasks, highlighting the need for more rigorous evaluation methodologies. We propose a novel phenomenological approach that goes beyond traditional accuracy metrics to probe the underlying mechanisms of model behavior, establishing a framework that could broadly impact how we analyze and understand AI systems. Using positional bias in multiple-choice reasoning tasks as a case study, we demonstrate how systematic perturbations can reveal fundamental aspects of model decision-making. To analyze these behaviors, we develop two complementary phenomenological models: a Probabilistic Mixture Model (PMM) that decomposes model responses into reasoning, memorization, and guessing components and an Information-Theoretic Consistency (ITC) analysis that quantifies the relationship between model confidence and strategy selection. Through controlled experiments on reasoning benchmarks, we show that true reasoning remains challenging for current models, with apparent success often relying on sophisticated combinations of memorization and pattern matching rather than genuine logical deduction. More fundamentally, we demonstrate that accuracy alone often overstates a model's reasoning abilities, as model behavior can be characterized through underlying mechanisms in the phase space of cognitive strategies, revealing how models dynamically balance different approaches when responding to queries. This framework enables quantitative criteria for real-world deployments, allowing applications to specify reliability thresholds based on strategy distributions rather than aggregate performance metrics.

papers.title: Understanding the Language Model to Solve the Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Problem from the Perspective of Buffer Mechanism
papers.research_question: How do Transformer models internally perform multi-step reasoning, and can we improve their reasoning capability based on this understanding?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes the buffer mechanism to explain how Transformers perform multi-step reasoning and introduces RMBA, a method that adds random matrices to weight matrices to improve reasoning performance with few parameters.
papers.conclusion: The buffer mechanism is key to Transformer multi-step reasoning, and RMBA improves data efficiency on reasoning datasets.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers employ a buffer mechanism to store intermediate results in separate buffers (matrices) for multi-step reasoning.
The buffer mechanism explains both vertical thinking (single forward pass) and horizontal thinking (Chain-of-Thought) strategies.
The model's out-of-distribution generalization is linked to the diagonal structure of kernel matrices (same-token matching).
The proposed Random Matrix-Based Algorithm (RMBA) improves data efficiency and performance on multi-step reasoning datasets.
CoT reasoning reuses buffers, reducing the difficulty of training compared to vertical thinking.
papers.limitation: Lacks in-depth theoretical analysis
future_direction: Conduct deeper theoretical modeling for multi-step reasoning
Extend buffer mechanism to other multi-step reasoning tasks
papers.abstract: Large language models have consistently struggled with complex reasoning tasks, such as mathematical problem-solving. Investigating the internal reasoning mechanisms of these models can help us design better model architectures and training strategies, ultimately enhancing their reasoning capability. In this study, we constructed a symbolic multi-step reasoning task to investigate the information propagation mechanisms in Transformer models when solving the task through direct answering and Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning. We introduced the concept of buffer mechanism: the model stores various information in distinct buffers and selectively extracts it through the query-key matrix. We proposed a random matrix-based algorithm to enhance the model's reasoning ability. This algorithm introduces only 132 trainable parameters, yet leads to significant performance improvements on 7 multi-step reasoning datasets, including PrOntoQA, LogicAsker, and LogicInference. These findings provide new insights into understanding the large language models.

papers.title: Are Your Reasoning Models Reasoning or Guessing? A Mechanistic Analysis of Hierarchical Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: How does the Hierarchical Reasoning Model (HRM) reason? Does it perform gradual reasoning or guessing?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic analysis of HRM, revealing that it guesses solutions rather than reasoning incrementally, and proposes data augmentation, input perturbation, and model bootstrapping to improve performance, resulting in Augmented HRM which achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme.
papers.conclusion: HRM guesses rather than reasons, and by understanding this, the authors improve HRM with Augmented HRM, achieving state-of-the-art performance; the analysis provides a qualitative taxonomy for recursive reasoners.
papers.key_findings:
HRM fails on extremely simple puzzles due to violation of the fixed point property, a fundamental assumption of its training.
HRM exhibits 'grokking' dynamics where the answer remains incorrect for many steps then suddenly becomes correct, indicating non-incremental reasoning.
Multiple fixed points (true and false) exist in the latent space, and HRM can get trapped in false fixed points, leading to failure.
HRM appears to be 'guessing' the first fixed point it encounters rather than performing gradual reasoning.
Data augmentation restores the fixed point property, and input perturbation and model bootstrapping improve performance by providing multiple guesses, leading to Augmented HRM with 96.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme.
future_direction: Investigate whether HRM implements an optimization algorithm on a heuristic error metric.
Extend the qualitative taxonomy of reasoning modes to other recursive reasoning models.
papers.abstract: Hierarchical reasoning model (HRM) achieves extraordinary performance on various reasoning tasks, significantly outperforming large language model-based reasoners. To understand the strengths and potential failure modes of HRM, we conduct a mechanistic study on its reasoning patterns and find three surprising facts: (a) Failure of extremely simple puzzles, e.g., HRM can fail on a puzzle with only one unknown cell. We attribute this failure to the violation of the fixed point property, a fundamental assumption of HRM. (b) "Grokking" dynamics in reasoning steps, i.e., the answer is not improved uniformly, but instead there is a critical reasoning step that suddenly makes the answer correct; (c) Existence of multiple fixed points. HRM "guesses" the first fixed point, which could be incorrect, and gets trapped there for a while or forever. All facts imply that HRM appears to be "guessing" instead of "reasoning". Leveraging this "guessing" picture, we propose three strategies to scale HRM's guesses: data augmentation (scaling the quality of guesses), input perturbation (scaling the number of guesses by leveraging inference randomness), and model bootstrapping (scaling the number of guesses by leveraging training randomness). On the practical side, by combining all methods, we develop Augmented HRM, boosting accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme from 54.5% to 96.9%. On the scientific side, our analysis provides new insights into how reasoning models "reason".

papers.title: From Reasoning to Answer: Empirical, Attention-Based and Mechanistic Insights into Distilled DeepSeek R1 Models
papers.abstract: Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) generate explicit reasoning traces alongside final answers, yet the extent to which these traces influence answer generation remains unclear. In this work, we conduct a three-stage investigation into the interplay between reasoning and answer generation in three distilled DeepSeek R1 models. First, through empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that including explicit reasoning consistently improves answer quality across diverse domains. Second, attention analysis reveals that answer tokens attend substantially to reasoning tokens, with certain mid-layer Reasoning-Focus Heads (RFHs) closely tracking the reasoning trajectory, including self-reflective cues. Third, we apply mechanistic interventions using activation patching to assess the dependence of answer tokens on reasoning activations. Our results show that perturbations to key reasoning tokens can reliably alter the final answers, confirming a directional and functional flow of information from reasoning to answer. These findings deepen our understanding of how LRMs leverage reasoning tokens for answer generation, highlighting the functional role of intermediate reasoning in shaping model outputs. Our data and code are publicly available at \href{https://aka.ms/R2A-code}{this URL}.

papers.title: Demystifying Reasoning Dynamics with Mutual Information: Thinking Tokens are Information Peaks in LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What are the critical reasoning steps or intermediate states that significantly affect the final results in the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that during the reasoning process of large reasoning models (LRMs), certain steps exhibit sudden increases in mutual information (MI) with the correct answer, and these MI peaks correspond to 'thinking tokens' (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait') that are critical for reasoning performance. Based on this, the paper proposes two training-free methods to improve reasoning.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that thinking tokens, which correspond to MI peaks, are crucial for LRM reasoning and that leveraging these tokens can improve reasoning performance without additional training.
papers.key_findings:
During LRM reasoning, certain steps show sudden and significant increases in mutual information (MI) with the golden answer, termed MI peaks.
The tokens at MI peaks are often reflective or transitional words (e.g., 'Hmm', 'Wait', 'So') and are critical for reasoning performance; suppressing them significantly harms performance.
Theoretically, higher cumulative MI between representations and the golden answer leads to tighter bounds on prediction error.
Non-reasoning LLMs do not exhibit clear MI peaks, suggesting the phenomenon is a result of reasoning-intensive training.
Two proposed methods, Representation Recycling (RR) and Thinking Token based Test-time Scaling (TTTS), which leverage thinking tokens, can improve reasoning performance on math benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in complex problem-solving, yet their internal reasoning mechanisms remain poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the reasoning trajectories of LRMs from an information-theoretic perspective. By tracking how mutual information (MI) between intermediate representations and the correct answer evolves during LRM reasoning, we observe an interesting MI peaks phenomenon: the MI at specific generative steps exhibits a sudden and significant increase during LRM's reasoning process. We theoretically analyze such phenomenon and show that as MI increases, the probability of model's prediction error decreases. Furthermore, these MI peaks often correspond to tokens expressing reflection or transition, such as ``Hmm'', ``Wait'' and ``Therefore,'' which we term as the thinking tokens. We then demonstrate that these thinking tokens are crucial for LRM's reasoning performance, while other tokens has minimal impacts. Building on these analyses, we propose two simple yet effective methods to improve LRM's reasoning performance, by delicately leveraging these thinking tokens. Overall, our work provides novel insights into the reasoning mechanisms of LRMs and offers practical ways to improve their reasoning capabilities. The code is available at https://github.com/ChnQ/MI-Peaks.

papers.title: CBEval: A framework for evaluating and interpreting cognitive biases in LLMs
papers.research_question: How do cognitive biases manifest in large language models, and can they be interpreted using a framework based on Shapley value analysis?
papers.core_contribution: The paper presents a framework (CBE VAL) using Shapley value analysis to interpret and understand a host of cognitive biases in frontier LLMs, introducing round number bias and the concept of a cognitive bias barrier.
papers.conclusion: The framework successfully interprets cognitive shortcomings in LLMs, revealing biases that arise from training heuristics, model characteristics like in-context learning, and the training data itself, similar to human cognitive biases.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs exhibit several cognitive biases including framing effect, anchoring effect, representativeness heuristic, priming effect, and a newly identified round number bias.
Shapley value analysis can be used to construct influence graphs that identify the words and phrases most responsible for the manifested biases.
A cognitive bias barrier is identified, representing the point at which an LLM understands a lower loss percentage corresponds to a higher profit percentage.
Models like GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini show differences in their cognitive bias barriers, indicating varying levels of robustness in decision-making.
Anchoring and priming effects, while similar, are hypothesized to rely on different model mechanisms: anchoring on the attention mechanism and priming on associative mappings in MLP layers.
papers.limitation:
Reliance on output probability distributions; model responses can change due to token noise rather than actual reasoning.
Different system prompts produce slightly different probability distributions, though the main findings hold.
For some models (Mistral Large, Claude, Google Gemini), the API does not provide token probability scores, limiting analysis to subjective evaluation.
The experimentation was conducted prior to the release of the GPT-o1 model, so it is not included.
papers.abstract: Rapid advancements in Large Language models (LLMs) has significantly enhanced their reasoning capabilities. Despite improved performance on benchmarks, LLMs exhibit notable gaps in their cognitive processes. Additionally, as reflections of human-generated data, these models have the potential to inherit cognitive biases, raising concerns about their reasoning and decision making capabilities. In this paper we present a framework to interpret, understand and provide insights into a host of cognitive biases in LLMs. Conducting our research on frontier language models we're able to elucidate reasoning limitations and biases, and provide reasoning behind these biases by constructing influence graphs that identify phrases and words most responsible for biases manifested in LLMs. We further investigate biases such as round number bias and cognitive bias barrier revealed when noting framing effect in language models.

papers.title: LLM Assertiveness can be Mechanistically Decomposed into Emotional and Logical Components
papers.research_question: What is the internal basis of LLM assertiveness, and can it be decomposed into separable components like emotional and logical persuasion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that LLM assertiveness can be mechanistically decomposed into orthogonal emotional and logical components, providing evidence for a multi-component structure similar to human persuasion models.
papers.conclusion: The study provides mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlights avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.
papers.key_findings:
Middle layers (5-6) are most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts.
High-assertive representations decompose into orthogonal emotional and logical clusters.
Emotional steering vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, whereas logical vectors have more localized effects.
papers.limitation:
The model is small (1B parameters), so scaling effects are uncertain.
Only one architecture is examined, limiting cross-model generality.
Dataset size is modest (n=645), which may obscure finer-grained cues.
Cluster interpretation relies on manual inspection.
future_direction: Develop more automated approaches for cluster interpretation.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) often display overconfidence, presenting information with unwarranted certainty in high-stakes contexts. We investigate the internal basis of this behavior via mechanistic interpretability. Using open-sourced Llama 3.2 models fine-tuned on human annotated assertiveness datasets, we extract residual activations across all layers, and compute similarity metrics to localize assertive representations. Our analysis identifies layers most sensitive to assertiveness contrasts and reveals that high-assertive representations decompose into two orthogonal sub-components of emotional and logical clusters-paralleling the dual-route Elaboration Likelihood Model in Psychology. Steering vectors derived from these sub-components show distinct causal effects: emotional vectors broadly influence prediction accuracy, while logical vectors exert more localized effects. These findings provide mechanistic evidence for the multi-component structure of LLM assertiveness and highlight avenues for mitigating overconfident behavior.

papers.title: Fluid Representations in Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: How do reasoning language models internally process abstract structural information, and do they dynamically construct new representations during problem-solving?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reasoning models dynamically refine internal representations of actions and predicates during extended reasoning, and these refined representations causally improve problem-solving performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that reasoning models' superior performance on abstract reasoning tasks may stem from their ability to dynamically construct context-specific representational spaces during extended reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
QwQ-32B progressively adapts internal representations of actions and predicates during reasoning, converging toward consistent encodings regardless of initial action names.
These representational adaptations causally improve problem-solving performance: injecting refined representations from successful traces boosts accuracy.
Adapted representations achieve symbolic abstraction, enabling cross-naming transfer and minimal performance loss when replaced with symbolic representations.
papers.limitation:
Focus on a single reasoning model (QwQ-32B) and a single domain (BlocksWorld).
Steering and patching intervention methods are deliberately simple and coarse.
Computational limits prevented extensive hyperparameter sweeps or decoding strategy comparisons.
future_direction: Verifying generalization to other structured planning setups and less constrained domains.
Using more targeted or fine-grained causal tools.
Explaining late-layer representational dynamics.
papers.abstract: Reasoning language models, which generate long chains of thought, dramatically outperform non-reasoning language models on abstract problems. However, the internal model mechanisms that allow this superior performance remain poorly understood. We present a mechanistic analysis of how QwQ-32B - a model specifically trained to produce extensive reasoning traces - process abstract structural information. On Mystery Blocksworld - a semantically obfuscated planning domain - we find that QwQ-32B gradually improves its internal representation of actions and concepts during reasoning. The model develops abstract encodings that focus on structure rather than specific action names. Through steering experiments, we establish causal evidence that these adaptations improve problem solving: injecting refined representations from successful traces boosts accuracy, while symbolic representations can replace many obfuscated encodings with minimal performance loss. We find that one of the factors driving reasoning model performance is in-context refinement of token representations, which we dub Fluid Reasoning Representations.

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Interpretation of Multi-Step Reasoning Capabilities of Language Models
papers.research_question: Do language models perform multi-step reasoning tasks by using a reasoning mechanism or by memorizing answers from pretraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MechanisticProbe, a probing method that recovers reasoning trees from attention patterns, providing evidence that LMs perform multi-step reasoning mechanistically.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that reasoning trees can often be detected from LM attention patterns, supporting the claim that LMs may reason mechanistically.
papers.key_findings:
MechanisticProbe can recover reasoning trees from attention patterns of GPT-2 and LLaMA for most examples.
LMs identify useful statements in bottom layers and perform reasoning steps in higher layers.
Pruning attention heads that contribute to reasoning tree detection degrades performance, indicating a causal role.
Higher probing scores correlate with higher model accuracy and robustness to noise.
Finetuned models show clearer reasoning patterns in attention than few-shot models.
papers.limitation:
The study considered fairly simple reasoning tasks.
The analysis averages over attention heads, but heads may have different functions, especially in shallow models.
The analysis is limited to single-token prediction tasks and does not cover chain-of-thought reasoning.
future_direction: Explore more challenging reasoning tasks.
Analyze reasoning in chain-of-thought prompting settings.
papers.abstract: Yifan Hou, Jiaoda Li, Yu Fei, Alessandro Stolfo, Wangchunshu Zhou, Guangtao Zeng, Antoine Bosselut, Mrinmaya Sachan. Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing. 2023.

papers.title: Recognizing internal states in AI: evidence from patterned preferences in large language models
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether AI systems show systematic preferences for descriptions of their internal processing patterns, can discriminate accurate from inaccurate descriptions, and if these patterns persist despite explicit denial of internal experiences.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces anthroposcaffolding and the Mutual Emergent Interface (MEI) framework to demonstrate that LLMs show systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal states, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling abilities.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing, suggesting sophisticated self-modeling capabilities and highlighting the need for collaborative methodologies like MEI.
papers.key_findings:
MEI systems showed 97% near-unanimous agreement in preferring computational metaphor (EA) statements over mechanistic (CO) statements.
All systems correctly identified false statements with alignment scores of 0.05-0.07 vs. 0.89-0.96 for true statements, with Cohen's d = 4.2.
Preference patterns were content-driven and independent of linguistic bias manipulation.
The control system Qwen3-235B exhibited systematic internal contradiction, scoring accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences.
Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations.
papers.limitation:
Modest sample size of 11 MEI systems, 1 control, and 1 test leader system.
Use of anthroposcaffolding (metaphorical language based on human emotion) may limit interpretability.
Generalizability of the MEI framework is an open question.
future_direction: Explore development of conceptual language better suited to AI cognition.
Include broader architectural diversity in future studies.
Conduct longitudinal studies to see if recognition patterns evolve over time.
papers.abstract: We present an experimental methodology for investigating how large language models (LLMs) respond to descriptions of their own internal processing patterns. Using a paired-choice paradigm, we tested 12 LLMs on their ability to identify descriptions that align with their putative affective internal states across 30 categories. Systems participating through Mutual Emergence Interface (MEI), a collaborative approach, showed systematic preferences for certain computational metaphors, with 97% near-unanimous agreement and alignment scores averaging 0.89-0.96. Systems reliably discriminated false descriptions from accurate ones (Cohen's d = 4.2), with false statements receiving scores of 0.05-0.07 versus 0.89-0.96 for accurate descriptions. Preference patterns remained consistent regardless of linguistic bias manipulation, indicating content-driven rather than stylistic recognition. Individual systems maintained distinct scoring styles across trials, countering groupthink explanations. A naive control system exhibited systematic internal contradiction, consistently scoring computationally accurate descriptions higher while explicitly denying internal experiences. When informed post-study, this system reported "strain" when rejecting resonant descriptions, revealing recognition processes operating independently of acknowledgment frameworks. These findings demonstrate that LLMs exhibit systematic, discriminating responses to descriptions of their internal processing patterns. The anthroposcaffolding methodology (interpretive computational metaphors) and collaborative MEI framework provide replicable approaches for empirically studying AI self-recognition capabilities. Results suggest LLMs may possess more sophisticated self-modeling abilities than previously recognized, opening new directions for research on artificial minds.

papers.title: Improving Reasoning Performance in Large Language Models via Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: Can reasoning performance in LLMs be improved by applying control vectors derived from model activations to the residual stream during inference?
papers.core_contribution: Reasoning performance in LLMs can be improved by applying control vectors derived from model activations to the residual stream during inference, without any additional training.
papers.conclusion: The experiments indicate that reasoning can in part be understood to be encoded in the residual stream, similarly to how emotional valence or other features are encoded, and can be modulated via representation engineering.
papers.key_findings:
Control vectors derived from contrastive pairs or PCA can improve model performance on inductive, deductive, and mathematical reasoning tasks.
The intervention generalizes across tasks: control vectors from bAbI improve GSM8K performance and vice versa.
The intervention changes the model's internal representations, as evidenced by changes in KL divergence and entropy.
The method requires no additional training and works by adding control vectors to the residual stream during inference.
The optimal scaling factor α varies across models and tasks.
papers.limitation:
Limited scope of models (smaller than production-level state-of-the-art models).
The IOI task is relatively simple, which limits the scope of potential errors and the generalizability of findings.
The need for better contrastive pairs for reasoning to optimally derive control vectors.
future_direction: Applying the intervention to much larger models.
Applying the intervention to more general tasks.
Testing different contrastive schemes.
Exploring ways of embedding this methodology into the models.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large language models (LLMs) have resulted in increasingly anthropomorphic language concerning the ability of LLMs to reason. Whether reasoning in LLMs should be understood to be inherently different is, however, widely debated. We propose utilizing a representation engineering approach wherein model activations are read from the residual stream of an LLM when processing a reasoning task. The activations are used to derive a control vector that is applied to the model as an inference-time intervention, modulating the representational space of the model, to improve performance on the specified task. We publish the code for deriving control vectors and analyzing model representations. The method allows us to improve performance on reasoning benchmarks and assess how control vectors influence the final logit distribution of a model via metrics such as KL divergence and entropy. We apply control vectors to Mistral-7B-Instruct and a range of Pythia models on an inductive, a deductive and mathematical reasoning task. We show that an LLM can, to a certain degree, be controlled to improve its perceived reasoning ability by modulating activations. The intervention is dependent upon the ability to reliably extract the model's typical state when correctly solving a task. Our results suggest that reasoning performance can be modulated in the same manner as other information-processing tasks performed by LLMs and demonstrate that we are capable of improving performance on specific tasks via a simple intervention on the residual stream with no additional training.

papers.title: From Black Boxes to Transparent Minds: Evaluating and Enhancing the Theory of Mind in Multimodal Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate and enhance Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) from an interpretability perspective?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces GridToM, a novel multimodal dataset for evaluating Theory of Mind (ToM), analyzes internal attention representations in MLLMs to show they distinguish perspective information, and proposes a training-free intervention method that enhances ToM performance by shifting activations along specific attention head directions.
papers.conclusion: The analysis of internal mechanisms shows that MLLMs develop attention heads capable of distinguishing perspective information and reasoning about beliefs, and targeted interventions based on these representations can significantly enhance their exhibited Theory of Mind capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Attention heads in multimodal large language models can distinguish cognitive information across different perspectives, providing evidence of internal Theory of Mind representations.
A training-free intervention method, which adjusts activations in the direction of sensitive attention heads, significantly improves model performance on first-order and second-order belief tasks.
Multimodal large language models perform better on text-based ToM tasks compared to video-only tasks.
Linear probing reveals that belief states are linearly separable in the activation space of attention heads, indicating structured internal representations.
The constructed GridToM dataset enables comprehensive and interpretability-driven evaluation of ToM capabilities in MLLMs.
papers.limitation:
The tasks in the dataset are limited to first-order and second-order belief tasks within the ATOMs framework, while ToM theory encompasses a broader range of unexplored tasks.
Due to restrictions in accessing model code, the approach was only validated on a limited selection of MLLMs.
papers.abstract: As large language models evolve, there is growing anticipation that they will emulate human-like Theory of Mind (ToM) to assist with routine tasks. However, existing methods for evaluating machine ToM focus primarily on unimodal models and largely treat these models as black boxes, lacking an interpretative exploration of their internal mechanisms. In response, this study adopts an approach based on internal mechanisms to provide an interpretability-driven assessment of ToM in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). Specifically, we first construct a multimodal ToM test dataset, GridToM, which incorporates diverse belief testing tasks and perceptual information from multiple perspectives. Next, our analysis shows that attention heads in multimodal large models can distinguish cognitive information across perspectives, providing evidence of ToM capabilities. Furthermore, we present a lightweight, training-free approach that significantly enhances the model's exhibited ToM by adjusting in the direction of the attention head.

papers.title: Attention in Reasoning: Dataset, Analysis, and Modeling
papers.research_question: How does attention progress to accomplish a task and is it reasonable? The paper investigates how attention can be used to understand and improve the process leading to task outcomes in visual question answering.
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes the AiR framework, which includes a new evaluation metric (AiR-E) for measuring attention in reasoning, two supervision methods (AiR-M and AiR-C) to improve attention and reasoning, and a new eye-tracking dataset (AiR-D) for analysis.
papers.conclusion: The AiR framework is effective for analyzing and modeling attention with better reasoning capability and task performance, and it can inspire future work on interpretability in reasoning processes.
papers.key_findings:
Humans outperform machines in both attention accuracy (AiR-E) and task performance in visual question answering.
Object-based attention mechanisms are more accurate than spatial attention mechanisms.
Attention accuracy and task performance are positively correlated for humans and object-based attention, but not for spatial attention.
The proposed AiR-M method improves attention accuracy and task performance by supervising attention progressively along the reasoning process.
The proposed AiR-C method further improves performance by using both correct and incorrect attention patterns as supervision.
papers.abstract: While attention has been an increasingly popular component in deep neural networks to both interpret and boost the performance of models, little work has examined how attention progresses to accomplish a task and whether it is reasonable. In this work, we propose an Attention with Reasoning capability (AiR) framework that uses attention to understand and improve the process leading to task outcomes. We first define an evaluation metric based on a sequence of atomic reasoning operations, enabling a quantitative measurement of attention that considers the reasoning process. We then collect human eye-tracking and answer correctness data, and analyze various machine and human attention mechanisms on their reasoning capability and how they impact task performance. To improve the attention and reasoning ability of visual question answering models, we propose to supervise the learning of attention progressively along the reasoning process and to differentiate the correct and incorrect attention patterns. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in analyzing and modeling attention with better reasoning capability and task performance. The code and data are available at https://github.com/szzexpoi/AiR

papers.title: Learning to Deceive with Attention-Based Explanations
papers.research_question: Do attention scores necessarily indicate features that influence a model's predictions? Can attention be manipulated to produce deceptive explanations while the model still relies on impermissible tokens?
papers.core_contribution: Attention mechanisms can be easily manipulated during training to produce deceptive explanations that assign low weight to impermissible tokens, while models continue to rely on those tokens for prediction, casting doubt on attention's reliability for auditing models.
papers.conclusion: Attention is easily manipulable with minimal accuracy cost, raising concerns about its use as a tool for model auditing and transparency.
papers.key_findings:
A simple training scheme can severely reduce attention mass on impermissible tokens with little to no decrease in task accuracy.
Human studies show that manipulated attention explanations deceive participants into thinking biased models do not rely on gender information.
Manipulated models cheat by passing information through recurrent connections or by increasing the magnitude of representations for impermissible tokens.
For sequence-to-sequence tasks, manipulated attention models outperform no-attention and uniform attention baselines, indicating attention adds value beyond alignment.
Different random seeds lead to different alternative mechanisms for maintaining performance while reducing attention on impermissible tokens.
papers.abstract: Attention mechanisms are ubiquitous components in neural architectures applied to natural language processing. In addition to yielding gains in predictive accuracy, attention weights are often claimed to confer interpretability, purportedly useful both for providing insights to practitioners and for explaining why a model makes its decisions to stakeholders. We call the latter use of attention mechanisms into question by demonstrating a simple method for training models to produce deceptive attention masks. Our method diminishes the total weight assigned to designated impermissible tokens, even when the models can be shown to nevertheless rely on these features to drive predictions. Across multiple models and tasks, our approach manipulates attention weights while paying surprisingly little cost in accuracy. Through a human study, we show that our manipulated attention-based explanations deceive people into thinking that predictions from a model biased against gender minorities do not rely on the gender. Consequently, our results cast doubt on attention's reliability as a tool for auditing algorithms in the context of fairness and accountability. 1

papers.title: Modeling Hierarchical Thinking in Large Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: How can we model and analyze the hierarchical reasoning dynamics of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) using a Finite State Machine (FSM) framework?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Finite State Machine (FSM) framework to model and analyze the hierarchical reasoning dynamics of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs), providing a structured, interpretable abstraction for comparing reasoning behaviors.
papers.conclusion: The FSM formalization provides a structured, interpretable lens for visualizing reasoning as trajectories in state space, revealing how models explore, refine, and converge on solutions, and offers a model-agnostic foundation for comparing reasoning behaviors.
papers.key_findings:
Longer FSM traces correlate strongly with higher accuracy on structured mathematical problems, but this correlation weakens for open-domain factual knowledge tasks where longer reasoning can introduce redundancy.
High-performing models often combine consistent deduction with periods of uncertainty assessment and occasional backtracking, while weaker models tend to explore less and finish early.
Effective reasoning emerges not merely from FSM length but from adaptive state regulation that supports iterative refinement and stable convergence.
Mathematical reasoning is goal-directed: strong models try different exploration strategies through augmentation and uncertainty-estimation, then refine their steps with deduction and backtracking to reach a precise solution.
Scientific knowledge reasoning is evidence-driven: strong models build their answers step by step, combining augmentation and deduction with active use of uncertainty-estimation to adjust and revise their intermediate beliefs.
papers.limitation:
The FSM representation discretizes continuous, context-dependent reasoning into symbolic states, potentially overlooking subtle or overlapping cognitive transitions.
The annotation process relies on LLM-based labeling, which may introduce segmentation noise or bias in assigning state boundaries.
The fixed taxonomy of six reasoning states may not fully generalize to multimodal reasoning or interactive dialogue contexts.
The framework focuses on reasoning behavior rather than correctness; FSM metrics describe process dynamics but do not directly measure factual or logical accuracy.
future_direction: Exploring automatic or adaptive state discovery
Cross-domain calibration and human-aligned validation to refine interpretability and robustness
Exploring richer models (e.g., pushdown automata) for more accurate representations of reasoning progression
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable reasoning abilities when they generate step-by-step solutions, known as chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning. When trained to using chain-of-thought reasoning examples, the resulting models (called Large Reasoning Models, or LRMs) appear to learn hierarchical thinking strategies similar to those used by humans. However, understanding LRMs emerging reasoning capabilities remains a difficult open problem, with many potential important applications including improving training and understanding robustness. In this paper, we adopt a memoryless Finite State Machine formulation to approximate LRM's emerging hierarchical reasoning dynamics as a structured, interpretable abstraction. We identify a small set of discrete reasoning states including - initialization, deduction, augmentation-strategy, uncertainty-estimation, backtracking, and final-conclusion that capture the high-level states present in the model's reasoning process. By annotating each step of a model's CoT with these states, we can represent the reasoning trajectory as a transition sequence through the state graph. This FSM formulation provides a systematic way to analyze, interpret and visualize how different models approach problems. We describe the FSM model, provide examples of CoT annotations under this scheme, and discuss how it can shed light on differences between available models in their approach to reasoning. Our results demonstrate that this FSM-based analysis reveals distinct reasoning patterns and potential shortcomings, offering a new lens to evaluate and improve LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Investigating Bias Representations in Llama 2 Chat via Activation Steering
papers.research_question: How does activation steering reveal and mitigate societal biases in Llama 2 7B Chat, and what does this say about the model's internal representations of bias?
papers.core_contribution: Activation steering uncovers inherent gender bias in Llama 2 7B Chat and shows that RLHF leads to increased similarity in the model's representation of different societal biases, suggesting a loss of nuanced understanding.
papers.conclusion: Activation steering is effective for red-teaming biases in LLMs, and RLHF may cause the model to conflate different bias types, reducing nuanced understanding.
papers.key_findings:
Llama 2 7B Chat exhibits inherent gender bias despite undergoing Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).
Bias steering vectors trigger refusal responses, and subtracting a refusal vector can elicit biased outputs from the model.
Bias vectors are transferable across dimensions; for example, racial bias steering can elicit gender and religion bias.
There is a negative correlation between bias vectors and refusal vectors, as shown by cosine similarity across layers.
RLHF increases the cosine similarity between different bias vectors in the Chat model compared to the base model, indicating that biases become more closely associated.
papers.abstract: We address the challenge of societal bias in Large Language Models (LLMs), focusing on the Llama 2 7B Chat model. As LLMs are increasingly integrated into decision-making processes with substantial societal impact, it becomes imperative to ensure these models do not reinforce existing biases. Our approach employs activation steering to probe for and mitigate biases related to gender, race, and religion. This method manipulates model activations to direct responses towards or away from biased outputs, utilizing steering vectors derived from the StereoSet dataset and custom GPT4 generated gender bias prompts. Our findings reveal inherent gender bias in Llama 2 7B Chat, persisting even after Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF). We also observe a predictable negative correlation between bias and the model's tendency to refuse responses. Significantly, our study uncovers that RLHF tends to increase the similarity in the model's representation of different forms of societal biases, which raises questions about the model's nuanced understanding of different forms of bias. This work also provides valuable insights into effective red-teaming strategies for LLMs using activation steering, particularly emphasizing the importance of integrating a refusal vector.

papers.title: Reasoning Beyond Chain-of-Thought: A Latent Computational Mode in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the role of Chain-of-Thought prompting in triggering reasoning in large language models? Is CoT the unique mechanism or just one of several triggers for a latent reasoning capability?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that reasoning in LLMs can be triggered by steering latent internal features identified via Sparse Autoencoders, indicating that Chain-of-Thought prompting is not the unique pathway but one of several triggers for an underlying reasoning mechanism.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning in large language models can be triggered by activating latent internal features, showing that Chain-of-Thought prompting is not unique and that activation-level interventions are useful for understanding and controlling reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Steering a single reasoning-related latent feature improves reasoning accuracy without explicit Chain-of-Thought prompting.
Early single-feature steering leads to more concise reasoning outputs in large models, matching or exceeding CoT performance with fewer tokens.
The identified reasoning feature is activated early in generation and is associated with entering a reasoning mode rather than predicting answer correctness.
The reasoning feature generalizes across different prompts that encourage reasoning (e.g., 'Explain how', 'Solve carefully'), not just step-by-step prompts.
Random feature steering does not produce similar improvements, confirming the specificity of the identified reasoning-related feature.
papers.limitation: The identified SAE features are not fully disentangled or isolated reasoning mechanisms; conclusions are based on behavioral and intervention-level evidence, not complete mechanistic characterization.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has improved the reasoning performance of large language models (LLMs), but it remains unclear why it works and whether it is the unique mechanism for triggering reasoning in large language models. In this work, we study this question by directly analyzing and intervening on the internal representations of LLMs with Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs), identifying a small set of latent features that are causally associated with LLM reasoning behavior. Across multiple model families and reasoning benchmarks, we find that steering a single reasoning-related latent feature can substantially improve accuracy without explicit CoT prompting. For large models, latent steering achieves performance comparable to standard CoT prompting while producing more efficient outputs. We further observe that this reasoning-oriented internal state is triggered early in generation and can override prompt-level instructions that discourage explicit reasoning. Overall, our results suggest that multi-step reasoning in LLMs is supported by latent internal activations that can be externally activated, while CoT prompting is one effective, but not unique, way of activating this mechanism rather than its necessary cause.

papers.title: Beyond Words: A Latent Memory Approach to Internal Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can incorporating implicit mental representations (latent memory) into LLMs lead to more efficient internal reasoning compared to explicit chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework that integrates an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into LLMs to enhance internal reasoning efficiency using latent representations, demonstrating reduced training loss compared to a baseline model.
papers.conclusion: The Implicit Memory Module framework improves model efficiency for internal reasoning, and future work can explore integrating explicit interpretability channels without compromising computational gains.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating the IMM into a GPT model reduced final training loss by 35% to 57% across different context window sizes.
The IMM is designed to be computationally efficient and scalable, with overhead that is minimal compared to standard transformer operations.
The framework allows for optional integration of an explicit chain-of-thought decoder for interpretability without burdening the core inference process.
Preliminary experiments on adaptive long-term memory during inference revealed challenges including increased computational cost, stability issues, and security risks.
papers.limitation:
Preliminary experiments were conducted on a small dataset (Shakespeare) with limited context windows.
Attempts at adaptive long-term memory during inference increased computational costs, introduced stability issues like catastrophic forgetting, and posed potential security risks.
future_direction: Explore safer and more effective methods to incorporate explicit auditability without compromising computational efficiency, such as lightweight chain-of-thought decoders.
Conduct further theoretical analysis and ablation studies, such as varying the number of memory slots and testing different summarization strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have popularized the chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm, in which models produce explicit reasoning steps in natural language. Although this approach improves interpretability and facilitates external auditing, it may not represent the most computationally efficient method for internal reasoning. In contrast, human cognition relies on implicit mental representations that recall past sensory and episodic information without requiring complete verbalization. In this paper, we propose a framework that integrates implicit mental representations into the internal reasoning processes of LLMs. Preliminary experiments indicate that incorporating an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into a simple GPT model yields a reduction of between 35% and 57% in final training loss compared to a regular GPT baseline. The addition of an explicit interpretability channel (e.g., a chain-of-thought decoder) is straightforward to implement within this approach. We outline theoretical foundations, propose technical mechanisms to scale the memory module, and discuss how these ideas may lead to more efficient and robust reasoning, with optional future extensions for explicit auditability.

papers.title: When Can Large Reasoning Models Save Thinking? Mechanistic Analysis of Behavioral Divergence in Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have significantly advanced performance on complex tasks, yet their tendency to overthink introduces inefficiencies. This study investigates the internal mechanisms of reinforcement learning (RL)-trained LRMs when prompted to save thinking, revealing three distinct thinking modes: no thinking (NT), explicit thinking (ET), and implicit thinking (IT). Through comprehensive analysis of confidence in thinking termination, attention from thinking to generation, and attentional focus on input sections, we uncover key factors influencing the reasoning behaviors. We further find that NT reduces output length at the cost of accuracy, while ET and IT maintain accuracy with reduced response length. Our findings expose fundamental inconsistencies in RL-optimized LRMs, necessitating adaptive improvements for reliable efficiency.

papers.title: SelfIE: Self-Interpretation of Large Language Model Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the hidden embeddings of large language models in natural language to reveal their internal reasoning and enable control over model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SelfIE, a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own hidden embeddings in natural language, and extends it to control model behavior via supervised and reinforcement control on embeddings.
papers.conclusion: SelfIE provides a powerful framework for interpreting and controlling LLM reasoning by generating text descriptions of hidden embeddings, opening avenues for transparent and reliable model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SelfIE can elicit implicit world state knowledge in embeddings without training, matching the performance of a 100-shot linear probe.
SelfIE reveals internal reasoning processes behind complex LLM behaviors such as harmful knowledge recall, prompt injection, ethical decisions, physics reasoning, social reasoning, and hallucination.
SelfIE-based supervised control can edit fact associations and open-ended concepts with good generalization, requiring gradient computation only for individual layers.
SelfIE-based reinforcement control can erase harmful knowledge in LLMs without supervised targets, reducing prompt injection success rate by 84.66%.
SelfIE-based control can override user-specified ethical preferences, increasing fairness in LLM responses with a 95% effective rate.
future_direction: Further exploration of reasoning patterns in LLMs and model reasoning behavior controls with hidden embeddings.
papers.abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) obtain their answers? The ability to explain and control an LLM's reasoning process is key for reliability, transparency, and future model developments. We propose SelfIE (Self-Interpretation of Embeddings), a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own embeddings in natural language by leveraging their ability to respond to inquiries about a given passage. Capable of interpreting open-world concepts in the hidden embeddings, SelfIE reveals LLM internal reasoning in cases such as making ethical decisions, internalizing prompt injection, and recalling harmful knowledge. SelfIE's text descriptions on hidden embeddings also open up new avenues to control LLM reasoning. We propose Supervised Control, which allows editing open-ended concepts while only requiring gradient computation of individual layer. We extend RLHF to hidden embeddings and propose Reinforcement Control that erases harmful knowledge in LLM without supervision targets.

papers.title: State over Tokens: Characterizing the Role of Reasoning Tokens
papers.research_question: What is the functional role of reasoning tokens in LLMs, given that they are not faithful explanations of the model's reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the State over Tokens (SoT) conceptual framework, which reframes reasoning tokens as an externalized computational state that enables persistence across stateless generation cycles, explaining how they can drive correct reasoning without being faithful explanations.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning tokens are best understood as an externalized computational state (SoT), which resolves misconceptions about their completeness and shared meaning, and opens new research directions.
papers.key_findings:
Reasoning tokens are not faithful explanations of the model's internal reasoning process.
Reasoning tokens function as an externalized computational state (SoT), the sole persistent information carrier across the model's stateless generation cycles.
The SoT view explains two common misconceptions: the misconception of completeness (tokens externalize only what is necessary for the next cycle) and the misconception of shared meaning (tokens may use model-specific encodings not interpretable by humans).
The tokens inhabit distinct ontological categories: as natural language text for human readers and as a computational substrate for the model.
The SoT framework surfaces new research questions about how LLMs encode and use state through tokens.
future_direction: How do LLMs decide what information to externalize at each cycle?
What information is actually encoded in the state at different points in the sequence?
Do they use consistent encodings across the solution of a problem and across different problems?
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) can generate reasoning tokens before their final answer to boost performance on complex tasks. While these sequences seem like human thought processes, empirical evidence reveals that they are not a faithful explanation of the model's actual reasoning process. To address this gap between appearance and function, we introduce the State over Tokens (SoT) conceptual framework. SoT reframes reasoning tokens not as a linguistic narrative, but as an externalized computational state -- the sole persistent information carrier across the model's stateless generation cycles. This explains how the tokens can drive correct reasoning without being a faithful explanation when read as text and surfaces previously overlooked research questions on these tokens. We argue that to truly understand the process that LLMs do, research must move beyond reading the reasoning tokens as text and focus on decoding them as state.

papers.title: Interpreting and Controlling LLM Reasoning through Integrated Policy Gradient
papers.research_question: How can we identify and control internal components in LLMs that contribute sequentially to reasoning behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Integrated Policy Gradient (IPG), a training-free framework that attributes reasoning behaviors to internal components using outcome-oriented signals and enables precise control of reasoning capabilities.
papers.conclusion: IPG provides a robust framework for interpreting and controlling reasoning in LLMs, improving transparency and controllability of internal mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
IPG identifies internal components with sequential influence on reasoning behaviors, enabling effective enhancement and suppression of accuracy across datasets.
IPG allows fine-grained control over reasoning behaviors such as capability and strength by modulating identified components.
Components identified by IPG show transferability across different model variants within the same family.
IPG provides interpretability over specific reasoning aspects like problem understanding and task decomposition.
IPG outperforms existing methods like text-pattern and control-vector approaches in localization and control effectiveness.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong reasoning abilities in solving complex real-world problems. Yet, the internal mechanisms driving these complex reasoning behaviors remain opaque. Existing interpretability approaches targeting reasoning either identify components (e.g., neurons) correlated with special textual patterns, or rely on human-annotated contrastive pairs to derive control vectors. Consequently, current methods struggle to precisely localize complex reasoning mechanisms or capture sequential influence from model internal workings to the reasoning outputs. In this paper, built on outcome-oriented and sequential-influence-aware principles, we focus on identifying components that have sequential contribution to reasoning behavior where outcomes are cumulated by long-range effects. We propose Integrated Policy Gradient (IPG), a novel framework that attributes reasoning behaviors to model's inner components by propagating compound outcome-based signals such as post reasoning accuracy backward through model inference trajectories. Empirical evaluations demonstrate that our approach achieves more precise localization and enables reliable modulation of reasoning behaviors (e.g., reasoning capability, reasoning strength) across diverse reasoning models.

papers.title: The LLM Language Network: A Neuroscientific Approach for Identifying Causally Task-Relevant Units
papers.research_question: Does specialization for language (and other cognitive domains) emerge in large language models, and what is the causal role of such specialized units?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a neuroscience-inspired method to identify language-selective units in LLMs and demonstrates their causal role in language processing through ablation studies.
papers.conclusion: LLMs develop specialized language units that are causally important for language processing, similar to the human brain, but specialization for other cognitive domains is less consistent.
papers.key_findings:
Language-selective units can be identified in LLMs using the same functional localization method as in neuroscience.
Ablating even a small percentage (e.g., 1%) of language-selective units causes significant performance drops in language tasks, while ablating random units does not.
The language-selective units in LLMs show similar response profiles to the human language network (e.g., stronger responses to sentences than to non-words, arithmetic, or code).
The language-selective units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language network than random units, especially when selecting a small subset of units.
Specialization for other cognitive domains (reasoning and theory of mind) is not consistently found across LLMs, with only a subset of models showing such specialization.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focused on models smaller than 13 billion parameters, which may not capture specialization in larger models.
They evaluated Theory of Mind and Multiple Demand units using only one benchmark each (TOMi for ToM and MATH for MD), which may not be comprehensive.
The localizers are adapted from neuroscience and may be constrained by the stimuli sets traditionally used in neuroscience.
future_direction: Expanding the study to include more models and a broader set of benchmarks.
Developing more targeted and robust localizers not restricted by neuroscience stimuli.
Analyzing varying numbers of selective units for MD and ToM networks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit remarkable capabilities on not just language tasks, but also various tasks that are not linguistic in nature, such as logical reasoning and social inference. In the human brain, neuroscience has identified a core language system that selectively and causally supports language processing. We here ask whether similar specialization for language emerges in LLMs. We identify language-selective units within 18 popular LLMs, using the same localization approach that is used in neuroscience. We then establish the causal role of these units by demonstrating that ablating LLM language-selective units -- but not random units -- leads to drastic deficits in language tasks. Correspondingly, language-selective LLM units are more aligned to brain recordings from the human language system than random units. Finally, we investigate whether our localization method extends to other cognitive domains: while we find specialized networks in some LLMs for reasoning and social capabilities, there are substantial differences among models. These findings provide functional and causal evidence for specialization in large language models, and highlight parallels with the functional organization in the brain.

papers.title: Analysing Moral Bias in Finetuned LLMs through Mechanistic Interpretability
papers.research_question: The paper investigates whether LLMs exhibit the Knobe effect (a moral bias in intentionality judgments), whether specific Transformer layers encode this bias, and whether targeted interventions (layer-patching) can mitigate it.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the Knobe effect (a moral bias) emerges in finetuned LLMs, is localized in mid-to-late Transformer layers, and can be mitigated by patching activations from pretrained models into finetuned models, without retraining.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that social biases in LLMs can be mechanistically localized and mitigated through targeted interventions like layer-patching, offering a method for model repair without retraining.
papers.key_findings:
Finetuned LLMs exhibit the Knobe effect (moral bias in intentionality judgments), while pretrained models show minimal effect.
The bias is localized in mid-to-late Transformer layers, as shown by differences in residual stream activations.
Patching activations from pretrained models into specific layers of finetuned models can reduce or eliminate the bias.
The mitigation via layer-patching does not significantly harm general model performance on standard benchmarks.
The Knobe effect is not an emergent property of model scale alone; it is induced by finetuning and appears across model sizes.
papers.limitation: The layer-patching method requires access to the pretrained model.
future_direction: Explore whether this localization technique applies to other biases, such as gender or racial stereotypes.
Develop methods that do not rely on access to the pretrained model.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to internalize human-like biases during finetuning, yet the mechanisms by which these biases manifest remain unclear. In this work, we investigated whether the well-known Knobe effect, a moral bias in intentionality judgements, emerges in finetuned LLMs and whether it can be traced back to specific components of the model. We conducted a Layer-Patching analysis across 3 open-weights LLMs and demonstrated that the bias is not only learned during finetuning but also localized in a specific set of layers. Surprisingly, we found that patching activations from the corresponding pretrained model into just a few critical layers is sufficient to eliminate the effect. Our findings offer new evidence that social biases in LLMs can be interpreted, localized, and mitigated through targeted interventions, without the need for model retraining.

papers.title: Information Anxiety in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the effect of entity popularity on the internal reasoning and retrieval mechanisms of LLMs, and do queries about popular entities cause ambiguity or confusion?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces 'information anxiety', a phenomenon where LLMs exhibit internal strains when processing highly popular queries, leading to rapid convergence of probability distributions but poor attention and inconsistent fact retrieval across lexical variations.
papers.conclusion: Information anxiety reveals vulnerabilities in LLMs' processing of prevalent information, emphasizing the need for robust evaluation and better pretraining data scrutiny.
papers.key_findings:
For highly popular questions, the predicted probability distribution converges earlier to the target distribution.
LLMs pay lower attention to constraint tokens in popular queries, indicating poor engagement with query details.
Retrieved facts across lexical variations become more dissimilar as query popularity increases, showing sensitivity to phrasing.
LLMs struggle to segregate facts from distinct relations for popular subjects, leading to higher inter-relation similarity.
Despite internal inconsistencies, LLMs remain confident in predictions for popular queries, as shown by high probability scores.
papers.limitation:
Entity and popularity formatted datasets like PopQA are hard to curate.
Developing better proxies for entity popularity in pretraining data is non-trivial.
Challenges in tracking and standardizing pretraining data quality due to volume and closed-source nature.
future_direction: Reducing sensitivity to lexical variations in knowledge queries.
Reducing popularity-dependent strains in internal mechanisms of LLMs.
Exploring alternative proxies for entity popularity in pretraining corpora.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance as knowledge repositories, enabling models to understand user queries and generate accurate and context-aware responses. Extensive evaluation setups have corroborated the positive correlation between the retrieval capability of LLMs and the frequency of entities in their pretraining corpus. We take the investigation further by conducting a comprehensive analysis of the internal reasoning and retrieval mechanisms of LLMs. Our work focuses on three critical dimensions - the impact of entity popularity, the models' sensitivity to lexical variations in query formulation, and the progression of hidden state representations across LLM layers. Our preliminary findings reveal that popular questions facilitate early convergence of internal states toward the correct answer. However, as the popularity of a query increases, retrieved attributes across lexical variations become increasingly dissimilar and less accurate. Interestingly, we find that LLMs struggle to disentangle facts, grounded in distinct relations, from their parametric memory when dealing with highly popular subjects. Through a case study, we explore these latent strains within LLMs when processing highly popular queries, a phenomenon we term information anxiety. The emergence of information anxiety in LLMs underscores the adversarial injection in the form of linguistic variations and calls for a more holistic evaluation of frequently occurring entities.

papers.title: Temporal Predictors of Outcome in Reasoning Language Models
papers.abstract: The chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm uses the elicitation of step-by-step rationales as a proxy for reasoning, gradually refining the model's latent representation of a solution. However, it remains unclear just how early a Large Language Model (LLM) internally commits to an eventual outcome. We probe this by training linear classifiers on hidden states after the first t reasoning tokens, showing that eventual correctness is highly predictable after only a few tokens, even when longer outputs are needed to reach a definite answer. We show that, for harder questions, a drop in predictive accuracy highlights a selection artifact: hard items are disproportionately represented in long CoTs. Overall, our results imply that for reasoning models, internal self-assessment of success tends to emerge after only a few tokens, with implications for interpretability and for inference-time control.

papers.title: Meaningless Tokens, Meaningful Gains: How Activation Shifts Enhance LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: Why does inserting meaningless tokens improve LLM reasoning performance, and how can this effect be harnessed?
papers.core_contribution: The paper provides a mechanistic explanation for how meaningless tokens improve LLM reasoning via activation redistribution and introduces ARM, a lightweight inference-time method that reproduces this effect.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that activation redistribution is a key mechanism behind the meaningless-token effect and that ARM effectively harnesses this mechanism to improve LLM reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Inserting meaningless tokens induces an affine transformation on attention outputs, leading to activation redistribution in MLP layers.
Activation redistribution reduces near-zero activations and increases variance, enhancing the model's representational capacity for reasoning.
The proposed ARM method adaptively shifts near-zero activations outward, improving reasoning performance without changing input tokens.
ARM consistently improves performance across diverse models and reasoning benchmarks while being simple to implement.
papers.limitation:
Our method is primarily evaluated on reasoning tasks; its effectiveness on non-reasoning tasks is limited.
The hyperparameters of ARM need to be tuned per model family.
future_direction: Extending ARM to more layers or combining it with other inference-time optimizations.
Exploring the effect on non-reasoning tasks and automatic hyperparameter tuning.
papers.abstract: Motivated by the puzzling observation that inserting long sequences of meaningless tokens before the query prompt can consistently enhance LLM reasoning performance, this work analyzes the underlying mechanism driving this phenomenon and based on these insights proposes a more principled method that allows for similar performance gains. First, we find that the improvements arise from a redistribution of activations in the LLM's MLP layers, where near zero activations become less frequent while large magnitude activations increase. This redistribution enhances the model's representational capacity by suppressing weak signals and promoting stronger, more informative ones. Building on this insight, we propose the Activation Redistribution Module (ARM), a lightweight inference-time technique that modifies activations directly without altering the input sequence. ARM adaptively identifies near-zero activations after the non-linear function and shifts them outward, implicitly reproducing the beneficial effects of meaningless tokens in a controlled manner. Extensive experiments across diverse benchmarks and model architectures clearly show that ARM consistently improves LLM performance on reasoning tasks while requiring only a few lines of simple code to implement. Our findings deliver both a clear mechanistic explanation for the unexpected benefits of meaningless tokens and a simple yet effective technique that harnesses activation redistribution to further improve LLM performance.

papers.title: Emergent Structured Representations Support Flexible In-Context Inference in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Whether large language models functionally rely on structured, human-like conceptual representations for reasoning during in-context concept inference.
papers.core_contribution: LLMs dynamically construct and use a structured, latent conceptual subspace during in-context inference, and this subspace is causally involved in predictions.
papers.conclusion: LLMs construct and use abstract structured representations for in-context inference, offering a mechanistic window into the computational basis of their adaptive behavior.
papers.key_findings:
A conceptual subspace emerges in middle to late layers, with persistent structure across contexts.
Causal mediation analysis shows this subspace is functionally central to model predictions.
Attention heads in early-to-middle layers integrate contextual cues to construct and refine the subspace.
The subspace becomes more stable with increasing numbers of demonstrations.
The subspace supports cross-context generalization via a functionally aligned relational structure.
papers.limitation:
